meta.title: "You said one thing — so you mean everything" — why your child loses arguments with their own words | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to reclaim their words and hold their position when their meaning gets twisted. Game-based course for children aged 10–16.

hero.headline: Is your child already defending themselves for things they never said?
hero.subheadline: She said one thing. She was heard saying something else. Now she has to defend herself against words she never said.

media.alt: A child whose words are twisted to an extreme

pain.title: Thought substitution: when what you said becomes something you never meant
pain.body:
"I don't like this subject" → "so you don't want to learn anything at all". "I don't like this" → "so nothing is ever good enough for you". At school, at home, in conversations. The child says something specific — and it gets blown up into something extreme. They feel unheard, but don't know how to explain it.

This isn't poor explanation or unclear thinking. It's distortion — deliberate or not: one idea gets stretched into "always", "everything", "never" — to make it easier to argue against. The child ends up arguing against a version of their words they never actually said. And that version is harder to defend.

The result — the child's position gets lost, even when it was perfectly valid. "Maybe I did mean that?" — and they either start justifying themselves or give up entirely.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 50 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Notices when their words are being stretched to an extreme
🧠 Separates what they said from what others "added"
💬 Calmly reclaims their position: "That's not what I said"
🛡️ Holds their point when someone tries to replace it with their own version

social_proof.quote: "So that means you think…" no longer throws her off. She's learned to say calmly: "No, that's not what I said" — and come back to her actual point.
social_proof.author: Oksana, mum of 10-year-old Daryna

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 10–16 year olds. At this age, children are receptive to new thinking patterns and are still forming their views.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
